stimulus.title: Two reactions in a blast furnace
stimulus.html:
Iron is made from iron(III) oxide in a blast furnace. Data at 298 K. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

Standard free energy changes at 298 K
ReactionEquationΔG° (kJ/mol)
1Fe₂O₃(s) → 2 Fe(s) + 3/2 O₂(g)+742.2
2CO(g) + 1/2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g)−257.2

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate ΔG° for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3 CO(g) → 2 Fe(s) + 3 CO₂(g).
parts.sample: Add Reaction 1 and three times Reaction 2 so the 3/2 O₂ cancels: ΔG° = +742.2 + 3(−257.2) = 742.2 − 771.6 = −29.4 kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how adding CO allows iron to be produced even though Reaction 1 is not thermodynamically favored.

rubric.point: O₂ is a shared intermediate: Reaction 2 consumes the O₂ made by Reaction 1, and the coupled ΔG° values add to a negative total, so the overall process is favored (Reaction 1’s own ΔG° does not change)
accept: coupling through O₂ makes the overall ΔG° negative
the favored reaction drives the unfavored one because their ΔG° sum is negative

parts.sample: The two reactions are coupled through O₂, which Reaction 1 produces and Reaction 2 uses up. Their ΔG° values add, and because Reaction 2 (tripled) releases more free energy than Reaction 1 requires, the total ΔG° is −29.4 kJ/mol and the overall process is favored.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the equilibrium constant for the overall reaction at 298 K.

accept: between 1.3 × 10⁵ and 1.5 × 10⁵, using ΔG° in J/mol

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Iron(III) oxide and CO can be stored together at 298 K for months with no detectable iron forming. Explain how this observation is consistent with your answer to part (a).

rubric.point: The reaction is thermodynamically favored (ΔG° < 0) but has a large activation energy, so at 298 K very few collisions have enough energy and the rate is negligible: it is under kinetic control
accept: favored but too slow because of a high activation energy
kinetic control; ΔG° says nothing about rate

parts.sample: ΔG° < 0 means the reaction is favored, but ΔG° says nothing about rate. The reaction has a large activation energy, so at 298 K almost no collisions between the solid and CO have enough energy to react. It is under kinetic control, which is why furnaces run at high temperature.
